hook: In 1798, an English clergyman named Thomas Malthus warned that people would always have more children than the land could feed. World population was then about 1 billion. By 2024 it was about 8.2 billion (UN, 2024), and food output per person had risen, not fallen. Was Malthus wrong, or just early?

options: How many people an area can support without damage
The number of people per square kilometer
The number of farmers per square kilometer of farmland
The share of land that can grow crops
prereq.why: Carrying capacity is how many people an area can support; it depends on technology and trade.

prereq.q: In which stage of the demographic transition model does the birth rate start to fall?
prereq.why: Deaths fall in stage 2; births start to fall in stage 3.

figure.caption: Malthus’s idea: population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8) and food arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4), so population outruns food.

chain.cause: Population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically
There is not enough food for everyone
chain.effect: famine, disease and war (checks) raise deaths

chain.cause: New seeds, fertilizer and machines raise crop yields
chain.effect: food grows faster than Malthus expected, which weakens his theory

chain.cause: Families choose to have fewer children as countries change
chain.effect: population growth slows, another critique of Malthus

ideas: Malthusian theory (Thomas Malthus, 1798): population grows faster than food, so famine, disease or war (checks) follow unless people have fewer children.
Neo-Malthusians, such as Paul Ehrlich (1968), apply the worry to water, energy and the environment.
Critiques: technology raised food output; fertility fell as countries changed; hunger comes mostly from poverty, conflict and how food is shared; trade moves food between places.
The idea links to carrying capacity: technology and trade can raise how many people an area can support.

misconception.wrong: Hunger in a country proves that its population has outgrown its food supply, as Malthus predicted.
misconception.right: Hunger often comes from poverty, prices, conflict and how food is shared. In the Bengal famine of 1943, the economist Amartya Sen found that food was available, but many people could not afford it.

summary: Thomas Malthus argued in 1798 that population grows faster than food, so checks such as famine, disease and war would follow. Neo-Malthusians extend the worry to other resources. Three critiques stand out: technology raised food output, fertility fell as countries changed, and hunger depends on access to food more than total supply.
